title: The Emperor's New Clothes
full_review:
In "The Emperor's New Clothes" (Paramount Classics), a slender what-if premise is turned into a pleasing historical comedy thanks to Ian Holm's superb performance as the short-in-stature but larger-than-life French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte.

The film imagines that Napoleon, in exile on St. Helena, arranged for a double to impersonate him so he could sneak back to Paris and reclaim the imperial throne. The egomaniacal Napoleon (Holm) switches places with foolish deckhand Eugene (Holm also) who becomes his stand-in on the island. On the island, Eugene is pampered and well-fed, preferring to dictate "his" memoirs, with every coarse thought recorded for history. Meanwhile, Napoleon has a tougher time off the isle. Even as an exiled monarch, he enjoyed the privileges of royalty. But, as he makes his journey to Paris, he must bear the humiliation of being treated like a mere commoner, first swabbing the deck of a rickety cargo ship then enduring an unbearable carriage ride sitting next to other commoners and livestock.

However arduous the journey may seem, Napoleon is driven by the thought that upon his return to Paris, France will once again rise up behind him. But he soon sees that times have changed.

Much to his dismay and disappointment, Waterloo has become a tourist attraction, where cheap trinkets and souvenirs of his famous battle are sold. The mood in Paris is also different, as the warm sentiments that once grew in the hearts of Parisians for the emperor have turned cold in the aftermath of his reign.

Worse yet, the conspirator he's supposed to meet in Paris has unexpectedly died. Napoleon is then taken in by the conspirator's widow, Pumpkin (Iben Hjejle), a beautiful but impoverished woman struggling to run a fruit-selling business. In one of the film's wittiest scenes, Napoleon turns the failing business around by applying his military savvy to dispatch �- with confident authority -� the local vendors through the streets of Paris.

His scheme to once again fly high as the Imperial Eagle goes awry when Eugene begins to enjoy the emperor's privileged status a bit too much and refuses to announce to the world he's a fake. At the same time, Napoleon can't convince anyone he's the genuine article. In a scene that is both tragic and comic, Napoleon temporarily finds himself in an insane asylum, where many other men claim they are Napoleon. Sorrowfully �- and ironically -- he discovers that his success may have led to his ultimate demise, wherein he has become the punch line of a joke.

As the film progresses, Napoleon begins a tentative relationship with Pumpkin, who, though she doesn't believe he's truly the emperor, sees the greatness in him nonetheless as an upstanding man. The film's humor therefore is replaced by a slight lesson on life's priorities and the healing benefits of the love of a good woman.

The film's first half is stronger, establishing the premise and allowing Holm to demonstrate his talent in playing Napoleon. (Twice before the actor flexed his muscles as the height-challenged emperor, first in a 1974 British miniseries and then in the 1981 film "Time Bandits.") With his hands firmly clasped behind his back, shoulders pulled back defiantly and chin jutting forward, Holm glowers at anyone one who gets in his way. He captures the emperor's puffed-up arrogance and self-importance, while still allowing for the film's gentle humor to come through.

Based on Simon Leys' novel, "The Death of Napoleon," the film takes a serious turn in its second half as Napoleon must choose between a miserable life as a man of great power, or a more personally fulfilling one with Pumpkin. For the most part though, "The Emperor's New Clothes" is entertaining enough to be a pleasant movie-going experience.

Due to an implied live-in relationship and fleeting crass language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG -- parental guidance suggested.

- - -

Navarro is on the staff of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' Office for Film and Broadcasting.
